chapters.situation: Gandhi is bedridden in London with pleurisy and has refused milk even when Gokhale pressed him to take it.
chapters.summary: Dr. Allinson, whom Gandhi knew from his 1890 vegetarian days, prescribes raw vegetables, brown bread and fruit, open windows, tepid baths and oil massage. Gandhi has a fanlight broken to let in air. Lady Cecilia Roberts kindly brings malted milk, believing it milk-free; Gandhi drinks some, reads the label too late, and stops, without guilt. Under-Secretary Roberts urges him to go home to India to recover, and he agrees.

updates.gandhi: Slowly improves under Allinson's diet and fresh air. Decides to return to India to recover.
updates.allinson: Twenty-four years after the London Vegetarian Society, treats Gandhi's pleurisy without milk.
updates.cecilia: Befriends Gandhi and tries to find him a milk substitute; her malted milk turns out to contain milk.
updates.roberts: Advises Gandhi to go home to India to be cured.
updates.pjmehta: Visits and offers to cure Gandhi if he will follow his advice.
updates.naturecure: Open windows, raw vegetables, oil massage and walks.
updates.diet: Gandhi unknowingly drinks malted milk, then gives it up without feeling guilty.

status.gandhi: Recovering from pleurisy, preparing to sail for India

chapters.situation: Recovering from pleurisy, Gandhi prepares to sail home to India for good after his years in South Africa.
chapters.summary: The Viceroy, Lord Hardinge, refuses a passport to Kallenbach, a German national in wartime, and the friends part painfully. Gandhi and Kasturba sail second class, since no third-class berths are free, eating fruit and nuts. He recovers on the voyage. He notices a deeper distance between English and Indian passengers, rooted in rulers and ruled. In Bombay, after ten years away, Gokhale has arranged a reception despite his own poor health.

updates.gandhi: Returns to India in January 1915 after a decade away, hoping to merge himself in Gokhale.
updates.kallenbach: Refused permission to go to India as a German in wartime. Returns to architecture in South Africa.
updates.kasturba: Sails home to India with Gandhi.
updates.jivraj: Had bandaged Gandhi's ribs with plaster, which Gandhi removes before the Red Sea.
updates.gokhale: Arranges Gandhi's Bombay reception despite poor health.
updates.racism: On board, Englishmen keep the distance of a ruling race.
updates.bombay: Gandhi returns to Bombay in January 1915, home after ten years.

status.kallenbach: In South Africa, separated from Gandhi

chapters.situation: Gandhi has landed in Bombay, but before telling his Indian story he goes back to his South African legal career.
chapters.summary: Gandhi never lied or coached witnesses, never made fees depend on winning, and warned clients he would not take false cases, so clean cases came to him and doubtful ones went elsewhere. In one complicated case the arbitrators' award favoured his client but contained a calculation error. Senior counsel refused to admit it. Gandhi insisted on doing so, and the client agreed: 'Let us lose, if that is to be our lot. God defends the right.'

updates.gandhi: Insists on disclosing an error that favours his own client, risking the case.
updates.law: Gandhi never accepts false cases or coaches witnesses, and charges the same fee win or lose.
updates.truth: Gandhi chooses truth over his client's advantage.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has insisted on admitting an accounting error that favours his own client, and must now argue the case himself before the Supreme Court.
chapters.summary: A judge asks whether admitting the error is 'sharp practice'. Gandhi objects to being accused before being heard, and the judge apologizes. Having the court's full attention, Gandhi shows the error was an innocent slip. The judges turn against the opposing counsel and correct the award rather than cancel it. Gandhi is convinced law can be practised without compromising truth, though the profession has a fundamental defect.

updates.gandhi: Wins by admitting the error. Shows law can be practised truthfully, though he still sees the profession as fundamentally flawed.
updates.law: The judges correct the arbitration award rather than cancel it.
updates.truth: Being frank wins the judges over.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is recalling how he practised law truthfully in South Africa.
chapters.summary: Gandhi practised as an attorney in the Transvaal so he could deal directly with Indian clients. When a client broke down in the witness box and his case proved false, Gandhi asked the magistrate to dismiss it, which only raised his reputation. He always admitted his ignorance and brought in senior counsel when needed. Clients' trust in him became trust in his public work, and many followed him into jail.

updates.gandhi: Drops a false case in court and earns even white lawyers' affection 'in spite of the handicap of colour'.
updates.law: Practises as an attorney in the Transvaal and openly admits the limits of his knowledge.
updates.satyagraha: Many go to jail on Gandhi's advice because they trust him personally.
updates.publicwork: 'Hundreds of clients became friends and real coworkers in public service.'

chapters.situation: Gandhi is recalling clients from his South African practice who became coworkers.
chapters.summary: Parsi Rustomji, Gandhi's longtime friend and client, comes to him in tears after being caught smuggling. Gandhi refuses to fight the case in court and advises full confession and willingness to go to jail as penance. He tells everything to the Customs Officer and the Attorney General. The case is settled with a penalty of twice the smuggled amount. Rustomji has the whole story written out, framed and hung in his office.

updates.gandhi: Saves a client by having him confess everything to the authorities.
updates.rustomji: Confesses smuggling, pays double the duty, and hangs a framed account of it in his office as a warning.
updates.truth: 'The shame lies not so much in going to jail as in committing the offence.'
updates.compromise: The smuggling case is settled out of court through full disclosure.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has landed in Bombay. His Phoenix settlers had gone ahead to India and are now with C. F. Andrews's friends.
chapters.summary: The Phoenix party has stayed first at Swami Shraddhanand's Gurukul in Kangri, then at Tagore's Shantiniketan, welcomed by the people Andrews calls his 'trinity'. In Bombay, Gandhi in his Kathiawadi dhoti and turban feels like a rustic in Jehangir Petit's mansion. At the Gujarati reception, where Jinnah and others speak in English, he politely protests and replies in Gujarati, and no one takes offence.

updates.gandhi: Welcomed in Bombay, he insists on speaking Gujarati at the Gujarati reception. Dresses in a Kathiawadi cloak, turban and dhoti.
updates.andrews: Places the Phoenix party with his 'trinity': Tagore, Shraddhanand and Sushil Rudra.
updates.shraddhanand: Treats the Phoenix party like his own children at the Gurukul.
updates.tagore: Shelters the Phoenix party at Shantiniketan.
updates.rudra: Opens his home to the Phoenix family.
updates.jinnah: Speaks in English at the Gujarati reception.
updates.pherozeshah: Gandhi takes shelter under his 'protecting wing' at the Petit reception.
updates.phoenix: The Phoenix party arrives in India and stays at the Gurukul, then Shantiniketan.
updates.dress: Gandhi wears a Kathiawadi cloak, turban and dhoti of Indian mill-cloth.

status.phoenix: Phoenix family now in India, at Shantiniketan

chapters.situation: Fresh from his Bombay receptions, Gandhi is summoned to Poona by Gokhale.
chapters.summary: The Governor of Bombay, Lord Willingdon, asks Gandhi to see him before taking any step concerning the government, and Gandhi gladly promises, since satyagraha means first trying to understand the other side. In Poona some members of the Servants of India Society hesitate to admit him because his methods differ, but Gokhale says he will regard Gandhi as a member regardless. He promises to fund the ashram Gandhi wants to found in Gujarat. At a farewell party Gokhale faints.

updates.gandhi: Promises Willingdon consultation before acting. Plans an ashram in Gujarat with Gokhale's backing.
updates.gokhale: Promises to treat Gandhi as a member of his Society and to fund the ashram. Insists on attending Gandhi's farewell party though too ill, and faints.
updates.willingdon: Asks Gandhi to see him before any action concerning government.
updates.sis: Some members fear Gandhi's ideals differ too much for him to join.
updates.satyagraha: A satyagrahi first tries to understand his opponent's point of view.

chapters.situation: With Gokhale's blessing for a future ashram, Gandhi visits relatives in Rajkot and Porbandar, travelling third class as a poor man.
chapters.summary: In a Kashmiri cap and simple dress, Gandhi is noted for a slight fever at a plague check. At Wadhwan he meets the tailor Motilal, who promises to go to jail if Gandhi leads. Everywhere in Kathiawad people complain of the Viramgam customs cordon. The Bombay Government blames Delhi, and when Gandhi later tells the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford, the cordon is removed within days. A Bombay secretary had called his mention of satyagraha a 'threat'; Gandhi calls this 'the advent of satyagraha in India'.

updates.gandhi: Travels third class dressed as a poor man and gets the Viramgam customs cordon removed through the Viceroy.
updates.laxmidas: His widow is among the relatives Gandhi visits in Rajkot and Porbandar.
updates.motilal: A tailor who earns what he needs in an hour a day and gives the rest to public work. He promises to go to jail if Gandhi leads. He later teaches tailoring at the ashram and dies young.
updates.chelmsford: Removes the Viramgam cordon after hearing Gandhi.
updates.willingdon: His government sympathizes but blames Delhi.
updates.viramgam: A customs cordon that harassed passengers, finally removed through Gandhi's efforts.
updates.satyagraha: Gandhi tells the Bombay secretary that satyagraha is no threat but 'a sovereign remedy'.
updates.thirdclass: Officials treat third-class passengers 'as so many sheep'.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has reached Shantiniketan to rejoin his Phoenix family, who have been living there under Maganlal's leadership.
chapters.summary: Gandhi meets Kakasaheb Kalelkar and admires how Maganlal has kept Phoenix's rules there. He persuades teachers and 125 students to cook for themselves without paid cooks, and Tagore calls it 'the key to swaraj'. Pearson throws himself into it with joy while students play sitar for the utensil-washers. The experiment fades after a while. Within a week a telegram brings news of Gokhale's death, and Gandhi leaves for Poona. He tells Andrews he does not expect satyagraha in India for about five years, having promised Gokhale a year of silence.

updates.gandhi: Introduces self-help cooking at Shantiniketan. Gokhale's death leaves him without his political guide. Is bound by a promise of a year's observation and silence.
updates.gokhale: Dies in February 1915, a week after Gandhi arrives at Shantiniketan. He had laughed at 'Hind Swaraj' and said a year in India would correct Gandhi's views.
updates.maganlal: Leads the Phoenix party at Shantiniketan and makes 'his fragrance felt' there.
updates.kalelkar: First meeting at Shantiniketan, where he teaches Sanskrit.
updates.tagore: Approves the self-cooking experiment and tells the boys it holds 'the key to swaraj'.
updates.pearson: Works tirelessly to make the self-help kitchen a success.
updates.andrews: Asks when satyagraha will come to India; Gandhi says perhaps in five years.
updates.kasturba: Travels to Poona with Gandhi after Gokhale's death.
updates.shantiniketan: A brief self-help kitchen experiment involving 125 boys.
updates.hindswaraj: Gokhale used to laugh at some of its ideas.

chapters.situation: Gokhale has died, and Gandhi hurries from Shantiniketan to Poona with Kasturba and Maganlal.
chapters.summary: At Burdwan the travellers are pushed aside at the booking window and find no room in third class. Gandhi and Kasturba take an inter-class compartment, and the guard makes them pay an excess fare all the way to Poona, only partly refunded later. Gandhi blames both the railways' high-handedness and the passengers' own dirty, selfish habits. At Kalyan he lets Kasturba use a second-class bathroom she is not entitled to, and admits it was partiality to his wife over truth.

updates.gandhi: Shoved and overcharged in third class. Admits a lapse in letting Kasturba use a second-class bathroom.
updates.kasturba: Shares the third-class ordeal. Her husband lets her use a second-class bathroom.
updates.maganlal: Gets a third-class seat and travels with Gandhi.
updates.thirdclass: 'Might was right' at the booking window. The guard charges an excess fare when there is no room.
updates.truth: 'A husband's partiality for his wife got the better of his partiality for truth.'

chapters.situation: Gokhale is dead. In Poona, the Servants of India Society must decide whether to admit Gandhi as a member.
chapters.summary: With Gokhale gone, Gandhi feels it his duty to seek membership of the Society. The members are split, some fearing his principles would endanger its aims. Rather than be admitted by a majority vote, he withdraws his application in a letter to Shastri. He later agrees the opponents were right about their differences, but they remain brothers, and he calls himself a member in spirit.

updates.gandhi: Withdraws his application to the Servants of India Society to spare its divided members. Remains 'a member in spirit'.
updates.gokhale: His death leaves Gandhi feeling without a pilot in Indian public life.
updates.shastri: Receives Gandhi's letter withdrawing the application.
updates.sis: Divided over admitting Gandhi; he withdraws, and their friendship deepens.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has withdrawn his application to the Servants of India Society and is travelling to see friends and learn about India.
chapters.summary: Bengali hosts in Calcutta stay up all night peeling nuts for him, and a deck passage to Rangoon is filthy. At the 1915 Kumbha fair in Hardvar, the Phoenix party under Maganlal takes on scavenging for the volunteers' latrines. Gandhi is besieged by darshan-seekers, which shows him how famous his South African work has made him. He sees hypocritical sadhus and a fake five-footed cow made by grafting on a calf's foot. He vows to eat no more than five items a day and nothing after dark, and keeps the vow for at least thirteen years.

updates.gandhi: Mobbed by darshan-seekers at the Kumbha. Vows never to eat more than five items a day in India, or after dark.
updates.ramdas: Travels with his father in Calcutta.
updates.maganlal: Leads the Phoenix party's scavenging work at the Kumbha.
updates.shraddhanand: Gandhi wants to meet him at the Gurukul near Hardvar.
updates.hardvar: The 1915 Kumbha draws a reported 1.7 million people, among them many hypocrites, some sincere pilgrims, and a fake five-footed cow.
updates.darshan: Gandhi is followed even to the bathing ghat and his meals, and finds being worshipped more painful than third-class travel.
updates.sanitation: The Phoenix party takes on scavenging, which they now see as their special work in India.
updates.diet: Vow: at most five items in 24 hours, and nothing after dark. No exceptions, even in illness.
updates.vows: The five-items vow serves as Gandhi's 'shield'.

status.gandhi: Famous in India; under five-items vow
